unit.title: Comply with the relevant legislative and regulatory requirements in hospitality

summary: This unit teaches you the main laws and rules that a villa, guest house or hotel in Jamaica must follow, and what you must do about them in your daily work. You will learn about tourism licensing, the Food Handler's Permit and public health inspections, the sale of alcohol, your contract, pay and statutory deductions, safety and fire rules, the protection of guests' personal data, and fair prices for guests. You will also learn how to find the current rules, keep records and speak up when something is not right.

blocks.p: Every villa and hotel works inside the law. Rules protect the guest who eats the breakfast, the worker who lifts the linen, the neighbour who lives next door and the country's name as a place to visit. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. It does not turn you into a lawyer. It teaches you the rules that touch your own job, who is in charge of each one, and what a careful worker does.

Laws, rates, fees and forms change. In this kit you will not find a tax rate, a fee or a fine, because any figure we printed could be out of date by the time you read it. When you need a figure, you **check the current rules** with the right agency and ask your supervisor.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers such as what a set of letters stands for, and essays) and group practical tasks. In the practicals you check mock documents against a compliance checklist, make a plain-words poster, prepare a new cook's compliance file and payslip, and role-play an inspector's visit and a telephone caller who asks for a guest's details.

blocks.note: Use only made-up names and numbers when you practise. Never use a real person's TRN, NIS number or ID in class work.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Why comply, and how to find the current rules

blocks.p: A **law** is made by Parliament. A **regulation** is a detailed rule made under a law, often by a minister or an agency. A **standard** is the level a property must reach, for example the tourism standards TPDCo inspects against. A **policy** is the property's own rule for how its staff apply all of these. You must follow all four.

ul: **Safety**: food poisoning, fire, falls and electric shock hurt real people.
**Fairness**: workers are paid correctly, guests are charged honestly.
**Legal right to operate**: no licence or permit can mean a fine or closure.
**Reputation**: guests read reviews, and one inspection failure or data leak can reach thousands of people online.
**Money**: fines, legal claims, lost bookings and repairs cost far more than doing the job properly.

blocks.p: Staff are not only watched by the law. Staff are part of it. A cook who works with an expired permit, or a front desk worker who leaves passport cards on the counter, can put the whole property in breach.

blocks.note: The JTB markets Jamaica as a destination. TPDCo improves the tourism product, sets and checks standards and trains workers. Do not mix them up: in the exam, 'who inspects the villa?' is TPDCo; 'who promotes Jamaica abroad?' is the JTB.
blocks.label: Remember

ol: Ask your supervisor which rules affect your job and where the property keeps its policies.
Use official sources: the agency's own office, website or notice. Do not rely on rumour, social media or what a guest says the law is.
Go to training: Team Jamaica, food handler's sessions, fire drills and safety briefings.
Write the date you checked a rule, so the next person knows when it was last confirmed.
When you are unsure, **do not guess**. Ask and then follow the answer.

blocks.p: A **compliance calendar** is a wall or computer calendar that lists every due date: licence renewal, each worker's Food Handler's Permit expiry, fire equipment service, pest control visits, tax and statutory payments, and training refreshers. One person is named for each item. It stops a permit lapsing because nobody noticed.

blocks.h: Registering the business and the tax number

ul: A new company or business name is registered at the **Companies Office of Jamaica**. A property cannot trade properly under a name that is not registered.
The owner and every worker need a **Taxpayer Registration Number (TRN)** from Tax Administration Jamaica. Employers use it to pay staff and send in deductions.
Staff also have a National Insurance Scheme (NIS) number, used for their contributions and benefits.

blocks.p: Businesses that serve visitors, such as hotels, villas, guest houses, attractions and tour operators, must be licensed as tourism businesses before they take guests. This applies to a small villa as much as to a large hotel. It does not matter whether the villa has run for a year or a week, whether it is high season or low season, or who owns it.

flow: TPDCo inspects the property against the standards
Licence is renewed and the property is re-inspected when the rules require

blocks.p: The inspection looks at safety, cleanliness, the condition of rooms, kitchen and facilities, and whether the property holds its other approvals (health, fire, business registration and tax). The licence shows guests, travel companies and the authorities that the property meets national standards. A property that runs without one, or lets its standards fall, can be fined or closed. **Owners should check the current steps and fees with TPDCo.**

blocks.note: A tourism licence lets the villa operate as a tourism business. It does **not** replace the other permits: it does not allow alcohol sales to under-age guests, does not excuse public health inspections and does not allow pay below the minimum wage.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Food safety: the Food Handler's Permit and public health inspection

blocks.h: Who needs a Food Handler's Permit

blocks.p: Anyone who prepares, handles or serves food or drink for other people needs one: cooks, kitchen stewards, servers, bartenders and housekeepers who prepare a guest breakfast. It does not matter how long you have worked there. It is **not** only for the head chef.

flow: Attend the food handler's training at the local health department
Meet the health checks the department asks for

ul: The permit is issued by the **local health department** (parish health department). Check the current steps, fee and renewal time with them.
It is valid for a set time. When it expires, you **stop handling food** until it is renewed. You never borrow a colleague's permit.
The employer keeps a record of every worker's permit and its expiry date. An inspector may ask to see them.
The purpose of the permit is to protect guests from food-borne illness.

blocks.h: What the permit means in daily work

ul: Wash hands properly and often; wear a clean uniform and a hair cover.
Keep cold food cold and hot food hot (cold at 5 °C or below, hot at about 63 °C or above, or as the property's food safety plan says).
Keep raw and ready-to-eat food apart.
Report illness such as vomiting or diarrhoea and stay away from food until the supervisor allows you back.
Never serve food that is past its use-by date, whoever tells you to.

blocks.p: A public health inspector may visit at any time, often without warning, to check that food is safe. The inspector is lawfully doing the job, so you receive them politely.

flow: Call the supervisor or chef at once
Walk round with them and answer honestly
Take note of any written notice and its dates

head: The inspector checks
Examples
rows: Cleanliness
Floors, walls, equipment, store rooms, hand basins with soap and paper towels
Food storage
Fridge and freezer temperatures, covered, labelled and dated food, stock rotation
Pests
Signs of rats, cockroaches and flies; how food is protected
Water, drains, toilets and waste
Safe water, working drains, how rubbish is stored and removed
People
Hygiene, Food Handler's Permits
Records
Temperature logs, cleaning schedules, pest control reports

ul: If problems are found, the inspector can order them **fixed** by a set date and, where there is a serious risk to health, can **close** the kitchen. Inspectors do not only give advice and do not cook the meals.
Do not ask them to come back another day, hide out-of-date food or refuse entry. This makes things worse.

blocks.note: A kitchen keeps records such as fridge temperatures and cleaning schedules to **prove** that food safety rules are followed. If it is not written down, an inspector cannot be shown that it was done.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: In Jamaica, report food poisoning claims or suspected outbreaks to your supervisor at once, so the property can act and the health department can be told where required.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: A bar, restaurant or villa needs the correct **spirit licence** to sell alcohol. Check the current licensing rules with the licensing authority.
Alcohol must not be sold to someone below the legal age, which is **18 years** in Jamaica. Confirm the current rule with your supervisor.
A person who is drunk must not be served more. Selling to a drunk guest can lead to injury, a fight or an accident on the road, and the property can be held responsible.

ol: If a guest looks young, **politely ask for photo ID**, such as a passport or driver's licence.
Check the date of birth and that the photo matches.
If the guest cannot prove age, offer a non-alcoholic drink. Do not ask the guest's friends how old they are, and do not serve 'just this once' because the guest is on holiday.

blocks.h: When a guest has had too much

flow: Notice the signs (slurred speech, unsteady, loud, spilling)
Refuse the next drink politely and privately
Offer water, a soft drink or food
Help arrange safe transport, and record it

blocks.note: Never serve a double to save the guest another trip to the bar, never let a guest pour his own drink and never serve drunk guests at a higher price. Each of these is still serving a guest who has had enough.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Mistake
Better action
rows: Serving because 'the guest is paying'
Politely refuse and tell the supervisor
Asking a friend to buy the drink instead
Refuse the drink; the rule applies whoever pays
Arguing with the guest in front of others
Stay calm, speak quietly, get the supervisor

sections.title: Employment: contract, pay, deductions and leave

ul: A new employee should receive a **written contract or letter of employment** saying the job, the pay, the hours and the main terms. A spoken promise from a co-worker is not enough.
Read it before you sign. Ask your supervisor to explain anything you do not understand, and keep your own copy.
Keep your **payslips**. They let you check that pay and deductions are right, and you may need them for a bank loan, a lease or a tax matter.
Check the current rules for the **minimum wage**, normal hours and overtime with the **Ministry of Labour and Social Security**, not social media or a colleague.

blocks.p: **Statutory** means set by law. The employer must take these from pay and send them, with the employer's own share, to **Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ)**. The employer cannot keep this money, hand it back at Christmas or pay it only if a worker asks.

What the letters stand for
What it is for

Income tax taken from each pay
NIS
National Insurance Scheme

Helps fund schools and learning

blocks.note: GCT (General Consumption Tax) is added to many bills and is paid by customers. It is not a deduction from your pay.

blocks.h: Reading a payslip: a worked example

blocks.p: The numbers below are **made up** to show the method. The real rates and thresholds change, so use the assessor's or employer's figures.

blocks.p: **Net pay** is what you take home. **Gross pay** is before deductions. Always add the deductions first, then subtract the total from gross pay, and check it twice.

ul: After a qualifying period of service, workers are entitled to **paid vacation leave** under the holiday rules. Check the current qualifying period and number of days with the Ministry of Labour and Social Security.
Public holidays have their own pay rules for staff who work on them, so the answer is never 'unpaid' by default. Ask the supervisor and check the current rules.
Sick leave and maternity leave also have rules; ask the supervisor and read the contract.

sections.title: Safety at work, accidents and fire

blocks.p: Jamaica's workplace safety rules place duties on both sides. Check the current law with the Ministry of Labour and Social Security.

head: The employer must
The worker must
rows: Provide a safe workplace, equipment and safe ways of working
Follow safety rules and training
Train staff, including in safe lifting, chemicals and fire
Use the PPE and equipment given
Provide the right PPE (gloves, aprons, non-slip shoes) at no cost to the worker
Report hazards, injuries and near misses
Keep a first-aid kit and trained first aiders
Never remove or damage safety items or alarms

head: Hazard
What the worker does
rows: Broken stair rail at the villa
Report it to the supervisor and mark it so nobody uses it; do not ignore it or repair it alone
Spilled liquid on a tiled floor
Put out a wet floor sign and wipe it up
Frayed cable or faulty equipment
Do not use it; switch off if safe; report it
Unlabelled chemical
Do not use it; ask the supervisor; read the label and the safety data sheet

flow: Give first aid and call for medical help if needed
Record it in the accident book or form
Report it to the authorities if the law requires

ul: The **accident report** (or accident book) records what happened, when, who was hurt and who saw it.
Never keep it quiet to protect the villa's good name, and never ask the worker to say it happened at home. Honest records protect the worker, the guest and the property.
Keep **exits and escape routes clear** and unlocked while people are in the building. Never lock fire exits at night to prevent theft and never store linen on escape stairs.
Fire extinguishers, alarms and emergency lights are checked and serviced on a schedule (service tags show the date).
Never switch off an alarm because it rings often; find the cause.
Every worker knows the assembly point and takes part in fire drills.

blocks.note: In Jamaica the emergency numbers are 119 for police and 110 for fire and ambulance. Display them at the front desk and in the kitchen.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Guest data protection and fair treatment of guests

blocks.h: What the Data Protection Act protects

blocks.p: Jamaica passed its **Data Protection Act in 2020**. It sets rules for how organisations, including hotels and villas, collect, use, store and share **personal data**. It is overseen by the **Information Commissioner**.

head: Term
What it means
Example at a villa
rows: Personal data
Information that identifies a living person
Name, passport number, email, phone number, photo, payment card details
Data subject
The person the data is about
The guest on the registration card
Data controller
The organisation that decides why and how data is used
The villa or hotel
Data breach
Personal data lost, stolen or seen by people who should not see it
A stolen laptop with the booking list

blocks.note: The villa's opening hours, the Sunday brunch menu and the number of rooms are **not** personal data.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Collect only what you need**, for a clear purpose. Do not collect extra 'in case it is useful', and never sell or give it to other businesses without proper permission.
Keep registration cards and files **locked away**, seen only by staff who need them. Never leave them on the front desk, pin them on a notice board or take them home.
Computers and phones that hold guest data need passwords. Do not email lists to personal accounts.
Treat **CCTV recordings** as personal data: they show people. Only authorised staff view them, and the villa keeps them only as long as it needs to.
**Destroy** old cards and printouts safely by shredding. Do not put them in the kitchen bin or use them as scrap paper.

head: Situation
Right action
rows: A caller says she is a guest's friend and asks for his phone number, email or room
Do not give any detail. Offer to take a message and pass it on
A guest asks to see the information the villa holds about her
Tell her politely that the manager will deal with it as the law says; do not refuse, and do not show her other guests' details
A laptop with the booking list is stolen
Report it at once to the manager. It is a possible data breach and may have to be reported
Someone asks to photograph the register
Refuse politely; refer to the manager

ul: Prices on rate sheets, menus and bills must be **clear and true**. Taxes and service charges should be shown as the rules require. Misleading prices can break consumer protection law.
The **Consumer Affairs Commission** deals with complaints about unfair prices or poor service.
Give correct bills and receipts.

sections.title: Acting on the rules and keeping records

blocks.h: When you are told to break a rule

blocks.p: Sometimes a supervisor, a guest or a colleague asks you to do something unlawful: serve food past its use-by date, falsify a temperature log, serve a drunk guest, give out a guest's phone number. Following orders is not a defence.

flow: Say you cannot do it and say why
Report it to the manager or the owner
Write down what happened, with the date and time

head: Record
Why you keep it
rows: Staff permits and certificates (Food Handler's Permit, first aid, Team Jamaica)
Show every worker is permitted and trained
Fridge and freezer temperature log
Proves food kept at safe temperatures
Cleaning schedule
Proves the kitchen is cleaned on time
Accident book
Shows what happened and what was done
Fire equipment tags and drill records
Prove checks and practices took place
Contracts and payslips
Prove terms of employment and pay
Payment receipts to TAJ
Prove deductions were paid

c1.title: A permit that ran out in Treasure Beach
c1.text: Mrs. Hyacinth Lawson owns a six-bedroom villa in Treasure Beach, St Elizabeth. Her cook, Mr. Carlton Reid, prepares breakfast and dinner for guests. On Monday morning the housekeeper, Shanice, sees that the date on Carlton's Food Handler's Permit passed two weeks ago. Carlton says that the new permit will be sorted out 'soon' and offers to borrow his sister's permit for now. A public health inspector is due to visit this month, and a family of eight arrives on Friday.

c2.title: The inspector arrives at a kitchen in Port Antonio
c2.text: At a small hotel in Port Antonio, a public health inspector walks into the kitchen at 10:00 a.m. with no warning. The chef is out buying fish. Kitchen steward Marlon is alone. He sees that the fridge temperature log has not been filled in for three days, and a tray of cooked chicken has been left uncovered on a counter beside raw vegetables.

c3.title: Payslips and a new waiter in Ocho Rios
c3.text: Kimberly Walters has started as a waiter at a hotel in Ocho Rios. She received a spoken offer from the supervisor and was told the paperwork would 'come later'. At the end of the month her payslip shows gross pay of J$90,000 with these made-up deductions: PAYE J$7,500, NIS J$2,700, NHT J$1,800 and Education Tax J$1,900. She is also asked to work on a public holiday.

c4.title: A busy night at the bar in Negril
c4.text: At a villa bar in Negril, bartender Devon serves guests on a Saturday night. A young-looking man orders two rum punches. Later, a guest who is slurring his words and bumping into chairs asks for a double rum and says his friend will pay for it. The owner of the villa tells Devon 'keep the drinks coming, it's a good night for sales'.

c5.title: Passport cards at a front desk in Montego Bay
c5.text: At a guest house in Montego Bay, front desk worker Latoya notices that registration cards with passport numbers are piled in a basket on the counter, where any visitor can see them. A woman phones and says she is the sister of a guest in Room 4. She asks for his mobile number and for the time he will be back. Later, a staff laptop with the booking list is missing from the office. The guest house also has CCTV cameras at the entrance.

c6.title: A new villa in Ocho Rios
c6.text: Mr. Andre Ellis plans to rent his inherited villa in Ocho Rios to visitors from next month. He asks the staff what he has to do first. The villa has a kitchen, a small bar and four employees. A hand-written list on the fridge shows what should be renewed and when, but nobody has been named to check it.

questions.q: What is the right action about Carlton's expired permit?
o: Carlton keeps cooking, since he completed the training before
Carlton stops handling food until his own permit is renewed
Carlton cooks only for the family arriving on Friday
Carlton uses his sister's permit until his new one arrives
questions.why: A permit belongs to one named worker and is valid for a set period. Once it expires, that worker must stop handling food until it is renewed. Borrowing another person's permit is not lawful.

questions.q: Which tool would best stop this problem happening again at the villa?
o: A notice asking each worker to remember their own expiry date
A rule that only the owner may look at staff permits
A compliance calendar with expiry dates and named checkers
A yearly reminder when the inspector arrives
questions.why: A calendar with named people and dates catches expiry in time. Relying on memory or on the inspector's visit is how permits lapse.

questions.q: Marlon is alone when the inspector arrives. What should he do?
o: Say that the inspector must come back when the chef returns
Put the chicken in the fridge and fill in the log before the inspector looks
Greet the inspector politely, let them in and call the supervisor or chef
Ask the inspector to wait outside until the kitchen is cleaned
questions.why: Inspectors may visit without warning and have lawful authority to check. Marlon should be polite, cooperate and call the supervisor. Asking them to leave, or changing records, makes matters worse.

questions.q: Marlon is tempted to fill in the missing three days of temperature readings. Why is this wrong?
o: It is a false record, and the log must show readings taken then
It would take too long while the inspector is waiting to see it
Only the head chef is allowed to sign the temperature log
Temperature logs are never checked by public health inspectors
questions.why: Records are evidence. Writing readings that were not taken is dishonest and defeats the purpose of the log. The right action is to be honest and start recording correctly.

questions.q: What is the main food safety fault in the kitchen that the inspector can see?
o: A staff member in a clean uniform and hair cover near the sink
A fridge that is switched on and has a thermometer on its shelf
A hand basin with soap, paper towels and a washing sign
Cooked chicken left uncovered beside raw vegetables
questions.why: Cooked food must be covered, kept at safe temperatures and kept apart from raw food. Leaving chicken out risks bacteria growth and cross-contamination.

questions.q: Kimberly has only a spoken offer. What should she ask for?
o: A written menu with the restaurant's opening hours
A written contract or letter stating job, pay and hours
A promise from the supervisor in front of two colleagues
A payslip dated before she started the job
questions.why: A written contract sets out the job, pay, hours and main terms, so both sides know what was agreed. A spoken promise is easily forgotten or disputed.

questions.q: Using the made-up figures, what is Kimberly's net pay?
questions.why: Deductions are 7,500 + 2,700 + 1,800 + 1,900 = 13,900. Net pay is 90,000 − 13,900 = 76,100. The other answers come from adding instead of subtracting or from missing a deduction.

questions.q: After taking the deductions from staff pay, what must the employer do with them?
o: Keep them in the villa's account until staff ask for them
Give them back to staff as a bonus at the end of the year
Pay them over only when the Ministry of Labour sends a reminder
Pay them to TAJ, with the employer's own share
questions.why: Statutory deductions are the government's money, collected by the employer. The employer sends them, with the employer's share, to TAJ by the date set in the current rules.

questions.q: Kimberly is asked to work on a public holiday. What is the best response?
o: Accept, since public holidays are always unpaid for hotel staff
Refuse, because hotel workers never work on public holidays
Demand double pay in cash at the end of the shift tonight
Ask the supervisor how holiday pay applies and check the current rules
questions.why: Holiday pay rules exist, so the supervisor and the current rules from the Ministry of Labour decide the pay. Do not assume it is unpaid or demand a figure you have not checked.

questions.q: What should Devon do about the young-looking man ordering rum punches?
o: Serve him, since a guest on holiday is not checked
Politely ask for photo ID and check his date of birth
Ask his friends how old he is and serve if they agree
Serve one drink only, and ask for ID with the second
questions.why: Anyone who looks under age should be asked for photo ID. Only proof of age is acceptable; a friend's word is not.

questions.q: What should Devon do about the slurring guest who asks for a double?
o: Serve a single drink and charge him a higher price
Serve it, because his friend is the one paying for it
Politely refuse, offer a soft drink and tell the supervisor
Let the guest pour his own drink from behind the bar
questions.why: Serving someone who is already drunk is unlawful and unsafe, whoever pays. The right steps are polite refusal, an alternative drink and telling the supervisor.

questions.q: The owner tells Devon to keep the drinks coming. What should Devon do?
o: Politely explain he cannot serve a drunk guest, and report it
Follow the instruction, since the owner is responsible for the bar
Serve the drunk guest, but water down his drinks a little
Leave the bar unattended until the owner changes his mind
questions.why: Following an owner's order does not make an unlawful sale lawful. Devon should refuse politely and explain; if the pressure continues he can report it or record it.

questions.q: Which licence must the villa hold to sell alcohol legally?
o: A spirit licence
A tourism licence only
A Food Handler's Permit for the bar
A business name registration only
questions.why: Selling alcohol needs its own licence, usually called a spirit licence. A tourism licence, a Food Handler's Permit and a registered business name are all separate.

questions.q: What should Latoya do about the registration cards in the basket?
o: Leave them in the basket so that filing is easier
Pin them up in the office so the manager can check them
Take them home to sort in the evening, then bring them back
Lock them away, seen only by staff who need them
questions.why: Passport details are personal data and must be kept locked away, seen only by staff who need them. Leaving them on a counter breaks the Data Protection Act.

questions.q: The caller says she is the guest's sister and asks for his mobile number and when he will be back. What is the right response?
o: Give his mobile number but not the room number
Give no details and offer to take a message
Give the details after she names his hometown
Tell her the time he will return but not the number
questions.why: A caller cannot be verified, and passing out contact details or movements can put a guest at risk. Taking a message protects the guest and still helps the caller.

questions.q: Why should the CCTV recordings at the entrance be handled carefully?
o: They are too expensive to store
They belong to the guests who appear in them
They show people, so they are personal data
They are used only for staff training
questions.why: Recordings of identifiable people are personal data and must be protected, viewed only by authorised staff, and kept only as long as needed.

questions.q: The laptop with the booking list is missing. What should staff do?
o: Wait a few days in case someone brings it back
Report it at once to the manager as a data breach
Email the booking list to everyone as a backup
Say nothing, in case guests cancel
questions.why: Lost personal data must be reported quickly so the property can act and, where the law requires, report the breach. Hiding it makes harm worse.

questions.q: After Mr. Ellis applies for his tourism licence, what does TPDCo do?
o: Sets the nightly rates he may charge guests
Registers the villa as a company
Collects the staff's statutory deductions
Inspects the property against the tourism standards
questions.why: TPDCo handles tourism licensing, including the inspection against the standards. Registration is done by the Companies Office and deductions go to TAJ.

questions.q: Someone tells Mr. Ellis that once he has a tourism licence the kitchen cannot be inspected. What is true?
o: The licence is separate: public health can still inspect the kitchen
The kitchen is exempt during the first year of trading
Only kitchens that serve alcohol can be inspected
Public health inspects only after a guest has complained
questions.why: A tourism licence does not replace health rules. Public health inspectors may inspect a kitchen at any time, with or without a complaint.

questions.q: The hand-written list on the fridge shows what needs to be renewed. What is the best improvement?
o: Add more items so that nothing is missed
Put the list where guests can read it
Name a person and a due date for each item
Ask the cook to check it once a year
questions.why: A compliance calendar works when each item has a due date and a named person. Without ownership, due dates pass unnoticed.
